newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Thorn profits up but outlook cautious.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Thorn profits up but outlook cautious.

text.p: British electrical retailer and rental firm Thorn Plc on Monday reported a modest rise in sales and profits for the six months to September, its first results since its split from long-term partner, music giant EMI.
Thorn reported a 10.5 percent rise in its six-month pretax profits to 87 million pounds ($145.1 million) on a turnover of 785.1 million pounds, up from last year's 733.9 million.
The pretax profit included payable finance charges of 7.7 million pounds, the company said. Thorn's earning per share edged up marginally by 1.1 pence to 12 pence.
The company's share price fell on Monday by 24p to 323-1/2p as analysts noted Thorn's cautious future outlook and said they were preparing to shave earnings forecasts.
Thorn's results were the first since its transformation into an independent public company after separating from its more glamorous music giant partner EMI in August.
Thorn's main business is hire-purchase deals on electrical goods but it is also sells furniture and personal computers.
Chief executive Mike Metcalf said the market remained highly competitive in most of its key markets including the U.S. and it faced delays in making cost efficiencies in Britain.
Metcalf said these factors would not stop it from achieving further growth in the second half, but was likely to "have some impact on the outlook for the next financial year."
Nick Budd, retail analyst with MeesPierson, described the outlook as "dull and dissapointing."
However, Thorn said it would make all efforts to expand its businesses to counter the sluggish outlook.
"We are looking at more expansion ... both through acquisitions and new stores," Thorn's group finance director Steve Marshall said in an interview.
Marshall said the firm was planning to make a capital investment of between 300 and 350 million pounds during the remaining six months of the current financial year.
"A lot of it would be spent on replenishing our assets," Marshall said.
Thorn was planning new expansions into rural areas of the United States.
"We are aiming for 400-500 places (stores) in the rural market over the next four to five years ... Even if that requires product innovation," Marshall said.
Chief executive Metcalf said the company added 15 stores, giving it a total of 62 rural stores in the United States.

Thorn's U.S. business, which grew 14 percent in the first six months, accounted for 35 percent of total sales. This fell below analysts' expectations of an 18 percent rise and a 38 percent share in sales.
The total rental-purchase market in the United States, estimated at around $3 billion, is expected however to show an overall decline over the full year due to tough market conditions, Metcalf said.
Thorn is expected to diversify into new products, some of them being new credit-based propositions, he said.

The company was also planning to introduce lease of furniture through Radio Rentals in Britain, where its turnover improved by only 2.1 percent with operating profit down 3.1 percent to 34.4 million pounds.
Metcalf said the company would contest any damages award with regard to law suits it faces in the United States over its rental-purchase sales system.
The law suits have depressed its share price in recent weeks from around 380p to 340 on what analysts said was "a hammering by U.S. investors."
The firm said it is not possible to gauge what level of provision, if any, would be required related to these cases. ($1=.5994 Pound)
